title: Electric Kettles With Auto Shut-Off: Three to Consider, and What They Can't Do
subtitle: A kettle that turns itself off can make a cup of tea simpler, as long as you know where the real risks still are.
excerpt: An electric kettle with auto shut-off ends the boil for you, but it can't stop a spill or a scald. Here are three to consider and the features that matter most for older hands.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A stovetop kettle asks a lot of you. You have to remember it is on and lift a heavy, hot pot off a burner. Many people look for something that takes a bit of that work off their plate.

An electric kettle heats water on its own base and, according to America's Test Kitchen, shuts off when the water boils. It also has a safeguard against running dry. That can make for a calmer routine. It does not make hot water harmless, though, and we will be plain about that below.
How an Auto Shut-Off Kettle Works

Two features matter most. Auto shut-off ends the boil once the water is hot enough. Boil-dry protection is a safeguard against the kettle running dry. The three kettles below are listed with these features, though the Breville listing is based on a partly cut-off page, so confirm it with the seller.
Some kettles have a cordless container that lifts off a powered base. The Breville below is one. It also has a 360-degree base.

Now the honest part. Auto shut-off ends the boil, and that's all. It does not stop spills, steam or scalds when you pour. A full kettle is still hot, and a cord-free pour can still burn. An electric kettle is also not a stove safety device. If the worry is a burner left on, a kettle won't solve that.

The lid matters more than most people expect. America's Test Kitchen found one Hamilton Beach model kept boiling because one edge of the lid stayed slightly open, so its shut-off never kicked in. The same reviewers warned about lids that pop open too fast:
"Dangerous Designs: We disliked models with lids that flipped back quickly and flicked hot water back at our hands." (America's Test Kitchen)

items: Both safety features: look for auto shut-off and boil-dry protection listed by name.
A lid that opens gently: America's Test Kitchen favored slow-opening lids and warned about ones that spring back.

Weight you can manage: America's Test Kitchen listed full-pitcher weights of about 6 lb 3 oz for the OXO and 5 lb 15 oz for the Cuisinart JK-17. We did not find a weight for the SoHo. Filling only halfway makes lifting much easier.
A readable water level: stainless steel pitchers hide the water level, so check where the gauge sits. America's Test Kitchen found the JK-17 gauge, under the handle, hard to read.
A handle that fits your hand: America's Test Kitchen said a bulky handle was uncomfortable for small hands on some glass models.
Controls you will actually use: the SoHo has one-button operation, while the Breville offers five temperature settings. Pick what suits you.

Fees: none of the three product pages showed a monthly fee or subscription. Be wary of store credit-card offers shown as a lower price. Home Depot's page shows one for the JK-17P1 ("Pay $44.99 after $25 OFF" on opening a new card), and that is not the price.
Warranty and returns: warranty terms vary, so check the box or manual and the store's return policy.

sections.content: Fill only as much water as you need. A lighter kettle is easier to lift, and America's Test Kitchen noted that filling to half makes lifting much easier for someone with weak grip.
Press the lid down firmly each time, then confirm the light changes when the kettle is on. The SoHo has built-in cord storage and a 36-inch cord.

If you have weak grip or hand pain, ask your doctor or an occupational therapist whether lifting a full kettle is safe for you. If you cannot safely lift a full pitcher, an electric kettle may not suit you.

Prices change often and differ from store to store. The Cuisinart JK-17P1 showed $99.95 on Cuisinart's own page in a search excerpt, against $69.99 at Home Depot, so check both. The Breville IQ has appeared at $129.95 (sold out) and $179.95. Warranties differ too: the JK-17P1 page lists 3 years, while Breville terms in search results conflict (1 year versus 2 years). Check the box or manual.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A good electric kettle won't do the pouring for you, but it can take some of the work out of your morning cup. Pick one you can lift comfortably, with a lid that behaves, and enjoy the tea.

products.name: Cuisinart SoHo Electric Tea Kettle, 1 L (CK-10TR)
products.blurb: A small, one-button kettle for someone who makes a cup or two at a time. It has auto shut-off with overheat and boil-dry protection, an exterior that stays cool to the touch, and built-in cord storage.

products.name: Cuisinart 8-Cup Stainless Steel Electric Kettle with Automatic Shut-Off (JK-17P1)
products.price: $69.99 (Home Depot, November 2026); Cuisinart's own page showed $99.95 in a search excerpt, so check both
products.blurb: A larger 1.7-liter kettle for households that boil more water, with cool-touch handles and an easy-open lid. Cuisinart's page lists boil-dry protection and a 3-year limited warranty. America's Test Kitchen reviewed the related JK-17, not the JK-17P1, and rated it recommended with reservations, noting its lid sprang back quickly and its water gauge is hard to read.

products.name: Breville IQ Kettle (BKE820XL)
products.price: $179.95 (Chef's Corner Store, November 2026); other retailers have listed it at different prices
products.blurb: The premium choice for tea drinkers who want five preset temperatures, from green tea to black. It holds 7.5 cups and has a cordless container and a 360-degree base. Its auto shut-off and boil-dry protection come from a search excerpt of a partly cut-off page, so confirm them before buying.
